title: The Real-Time Mandate

scenario.situation: The CEO asked for "real-time" sales dashboards. The lead engineer has scoped a Kafka + Flink streaming pipeline to push every order event to the dashboard within seconds.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The lead is convinced the business needs true real-time streaming and that a batch pipeline would be seen as second-rate.
scenario.question: Does the business actually need streaming, or would a right-sized batch pipeline meet the real requirement?

decisions.prompt: Before committing to an architecture, how do you scope the pipeline?

options.label: Build the Kafka + Flink streaming pipeline the lead scoped
options.detail: Accept the streaming design and start implementing it.
options.consequence: You commit engineering months to a streaming stack before anyone has defined how fresh the data must actually be. The hardest architecture is now locked in on an unexamined premise.
options.divergenceCost: Committed to streaming before establishing the freshness requirement it's meant to satisfy.

options.label: Interview the dashboard's users to derive the freshness SLA from how decisions are made
options.detail: Find out who reads the dashboard, how often, and what actions the data drives — then translate that into a freshness target.
options.consequence: You learn merchandisers review the dashboard once each morning and act on it in weekly planning; no decision hinges on sub-hour freshness. The real requirement is 'fresh by 8am', not 'within seconds'.

options.label: Benchmark Kafka against a competing streaming engine
options.detail: Run a bake-off between streaming frameworks to pick the best one.
options.consequence: You spend a week comparing streaming engines — a careful answer to a question no one has confirmed needs asking.
options.divergenceCost: Optimized the choice of streaming tool without confirming streaming is required at all.

options.label: Ship a nightly batch to be safe and revisit later
options.detail: Default to the simplest batch you can and move on.
options.consequence: You pick batch by gut rather than evidence; if a few views genuinely need intraday freshness, you'll have guessed wrong in the other direction.
options.divergenceCost: Picked batch by default instead of deriving the freshness the dashboard actually needs.

decisions.prompt: You've gathered how the dashboard is used. Which signal do you trust to set the pipeline's freshness target?

artifact.title: Data latency by design (minutes — lower is fresher)
artifact.caption: Streaming is 'freshest' on paper. But fresher-than-needed is wasted — the question isn't which is fastest, it's which is fast enough for how the data is actually used.

options.label: Pick the design with the lowest data latency
options.detail: Choose whichever architecture gets data to the dashboard soonest.
options.consequence: Streaming wins the raw-latency contest, so you choose it — optimizing a number the business never asked to minimize, and taking on 24/7 operational load for freshness no one consumes.
options.divergenceCost: Chose on raw latency alone, optimizing a metric the use case doesn't reward.

options.label: Compare each design's freshness against the decision cadence it serves
options.detail: Line each option's freshness up against the once-daily, 8am-deadline review the dashboard drives, and weigh cost and on-call load.
options.consequence: Against a once-daily review with an 8am deadline, every design fresher than 'hourly' clears the bar. An hourly batch meets the SLA at a fraction of the cost and none of streaming's 24/7 on-call burden — the extra freshness is entirely unconsumed.

artifact.title: Cost + on-call load by design (indexed) — all meet the daily SLA except nightly
artifact.caption: Every design at 'hourly' or fresher clears the once-daily SLA. Hourly batch meets it at ~1/5 the cost of streaming and none of the 24/7 on-call load — nightly is the only one that misses the 8am deadline.

decisions.prompt: What do you recommend to the lead and the CEO?

options.label: "Streaming is the modern standard — let's proceed with Kafka + Flink."
options.detail: Endorse the streaming build as the right, future-proof choice.
options.consequence: You deliver the impressive-sounding architecture, but sign the team up for permanent streaming operations to serve a dashboard read once a day. The cost lands later, quietly, as on-call fatigue and cloud spend.
options.divergenceCost: Recommended the trend over the requirement, buying permanent ops cost for unused freshness.

options.label: "An hourly batch meets the SLA at a fraction of the cost — here's the tradeoff, and the trigger to upgrade if a true intraday need appears."
options.detail: Recommend the right-sized batch, name what streaming would buy (and that nothing currently consumes it), and define when to revisit.
options.consequence: You give leadership a design matched to how the data is used, an explicit note that streaming buys freshness no current decision consumes, and a clear trigger to upgrade later. 'Real-time' becomes 'fresh enough, far cheaper, and easy to evolve.'

insight: The 'real-time' mandate was a phrasing, not a requirement: the dashboard drives a once-daily decision with an 8am deadline, so any pipeline fresher than hourly already meets it. Streaming would have delivered seconds-fresh data that no decision consumes, in exchange for permanent 24/7 operational load and several times the cost. The lesson is to derive the freshness SLA from the decision cadence the data serves, not from the loudest adjective in the request — matching the tool to the real need is the senior move, not defaulting to the most powerful stack.
